title: Animated Movie ‘Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself’ Boarded by Epsilon Film (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Epsilon Film has acquired worldwide rights to “Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself,” an animated family adventure movie based on “Petronella Applesauce
body:
Epsilon Film has acquired worldwide rights to “Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself,” an animated family adventure movie based on “Petronella Applesauce,” one of Germany’s most successful children’s book series.

	Epsilon Film will launch international sales on “Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself” at the American Film Market, which runs Nov. 10-15 in Los Angeles, where buyers will get a first look at footage from the movie.
	

	“Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself,” which is produced by the team behind “The Elfkins” and “Rabbit Academy,” centers on two children who are magically shrunk into a miniature world.


	“Blending fantasy, humor, suspense and adventure with an emotional story about empathy and overcoming prejudice, ‘Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself’ brings the beloved literary franchise to the big screen in a magical family adventure with international appeal,” said Epsilon Film in a statement.

	Alice von Einem, managing director of Epsilon Film, said, “What immediately captured our imagination was the idea of two children suddenly finding themselves shrunk into Petronella’s enchanted garden and experiencing an entirely new world from a tiny perspective. The film combines a highly commercial adventure premise with universal themes of friendship, courage and belonging, making it a wonderful family event for audiences around the world.”

	The film is directed by Ute von Münchow-Pohl (“The Elfkins,” “Rabbit Academy”) and Felix Schichl. The screenplay is by Claudio Winter (“The Elfkins,” “Rabbit Academy”) and Seraina Nyikos.
	

	Character design is by Oliver Kurth (“Monster Family 2,” “Grand Prix of Europe”). The producers are Dirk Beinhold and Valentin Greulich for Akkord Film, the animation studio behind “The Elfkins” and “Rabbit Academy.” Co-production partners include Seru Animation (“My Fairy Troublemaker”), PFX (“The Whalesinger”), VAST and JewelLabs Pictures. Tobis Film will distribute the film widely in German theaters.

	At AFM, Epsilon Film will be based at Suite No. 334, the Fairmont Century Plaza Hotel, Los Angeles.

schema.headline: Animated Movie ‘Apple Cadabra – I Shrunk Myself’ Boarded by Epsilon Film (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Star Flops and Slowing Investment Help Explain China’s Thin Festival Presence, Says Tokyo Programming Director
description: Star-driven flops at the Chinese box office, slowing investment and a reportedly more complicated censorship process have a bearing on China’s low
body:
Star-driven flops at the Chinese box office, slowing investment and a reportedly more complicated censorship process have a bearing on China’s low profile at international festivals this year, according to Ichiyama Shozo, programming director of the Tokyo International Film Festival.

	“In the past, casting a star in the leading role could guarantee a certain degree of success, but this year, many films featuring star actors have flopped at the box office,” Ichiyama tells Variety.
	

	Investment has slowed, he says, and many titles are reportedly sitting unreleased as censorship has grown more complex. All of that, in his view, has something to do with the absence of a strong Chinese showing on the festival circuit in 2026.


	Ichiyama has worked closely with Chinese-language auteurs including Hou Hsiao-hsien and Jia Zhangke, and says the mainland industry changed sharply in the mid-2000s. As the economy boomed, multiplexes multiplied and box office prospects rose, even independent projects with no stars attached could raise reasonable budgets in China.

	Taiwan, by contrast, looks comparatively steady. Its home market has always been small, Ichiyama says, but a range of public support mechanisms keeps production going.

	This year’s lineup is marked by films about historical events, wars among them, Ichiyama says. They include Samuele Rossi’s Competition entry “Even If Hell Came,” which follows a young Italian partisan holding out in the Alps in the winter of 1944.

	“I believe this reflects a global trend, as symbolized by the films dealing with the Second World War that were screened at this year’s Cannes Film Festival,” he says.
	

	Most of these filmmakers, he believes, look back at past events as a way to examine a world that is growing more divided.

	Tokyo’s Competition requires at least an Asian premiere, but the festival pushes for world premieres, and the split between the two usually lands at around half and half. The festival also aims for around half of the 15 films to come from Asia. Emerging directors expected to shape the future of world cinema get priority over established names, though veterans are not shut out. This year’s lineup includes veterans such as Garin Nugroho (“Red Before Dawn”), Milcho Manchevski (“Sister Brother Manhole Cover”) and Bahman Ghobadi (“Trees Are Watching”). Ichiyama says the established directors in the selection are reaching for something different from their earlier work.

	“We hope that our competition will serve as a platform for discovery,” he says.

	The Japanese titles in Competition, among them Ikeda Akira’s “The Canary’s Lullaby” and Yamamoto Akira’s “The Intertwining,” sit alongside those in the Nippon Cinema Now section. Ichiyama describes these filmmakers as lacking an international reputation so far but deserving of worldwide recognition. The Japanese films in the Gala Selection, including opener “Sukiyaki” from Zeze Takahisa, Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” and Sode Yukiko’s “All the Lovers in the Night,” work with bigger budgets and commercial demands while holding on to an auteur sensibility.

	“This demonstrates that the current state of Japanese cinema is in a very healthy condition. I think there are a surprisingly large number of talented filmmakers in Japan. The immediate challenge is to provide support for films by young directors, many of which are produced on a very low budget,” Ichiyama says. “While support for Japanese cinema has increased in various forms over the past few years, support for low-budget films is still insufficient.”

	Before Ichiyama became programming director, Tokyo lacked, he says, two things many festivals worldwide offer: backing for film production and education programs to train the industry’s future talent. Busan, in his view, was the first festival in Asia to introduce both.

	Tokyo is now trying to close that gap. Last year it launched the Asian Students’ Film Conference, which screens student work from East and Southeast Asia, and this year it added TIFF Work-in-Progress, a program for Japanese films looking for money to finish production.
	

	“Of course, this is not yet enough,” Ichiyama says.

	The task for the next five years, he says, is to take that approach further.

schema.headline: Star Flops and Slowing Investment Help Explain China’s Thin Festival Presence, Says Tokyo Programming Director

title: ‘VelociPastor 2’ Leaves FilmQuest Audience Roaring, Celebrating Human-Made Films in an AI Era
description: Who knew that one of this year’s giddiest celebrations of filmmaking would be a movie where the stunt dummies are obvious, the dinosaur costumes ar
body:
Who knew that one of this year’s giddiest celebrations of filmmaking would be a movie where the stunt dummies are obvious, the dinosaur costumes are obviously homemade and you can literally see the strings on special effects shots?

	That’s the joy of “VelociPastor 2,” the long-awaited sequel to 2017’s “The VelociPastor.” The first film was a modern cult comedy classic made on a $36,000 budget, which followed the adventures of Doug Jones (Gregory James Cohan), a man of God who turns into a bloodthirsty dinosaur while he’s cleaning up his neighborhood from pimps and drug dealers, and his girlfriend Carol (Alyssa Kempinski). 
	

	“VelociPastor 2” is even more ambitious, moving the action to “Italy” and spinning a yarn of a giallo-esque killer who is targeting area virgins. While the scope has widened, the low budget still keeps things charmingly ramshackle. Even after raising $118,297 on Kickstarter, all of the seams are still showing. But the effect is a tribute to low-budget filmmaking, poking fun at everything from wild inconsistencies that any script supervisor would have caught (the opening scene features Doug putting on a crucifix again and again) to wildly long pieces of exposition delivered via ADR.


	The Sunday FilmQuest screening of “VelociPastor 2,” a festival known for attracting audiences filled with indie filmmakers, was primed to enjoy the movie and laughed boisterously throughout. Beyond the jabs at the joys and flaws of low-budget filmmaking, the movie is filled with plenty of other jokes in the spirit of “Airplane!” that kept spirits high.
	

	There was also a sense of gratitude that so many of the jokes showed affection for the “let’s put on a show” enthusiasm that inspires both films. A frequent topic of discussion at the Provo, Utah-based festival has been the infiltration of AI in the industry, which is met with near-universal distrust and disinterest. In fact, one of the biggest applause points before every screening at the fest is a promise that the feature presentation doesn’t include AI.

	But the joy of “VelociPastor 2” is the knowing silliness of low-budget filmmaking gone wrong, something that would be too complex to try to craft an AI prompt. Whether it’s miniatures that don’t show the true scope of Italian city life or two extras playing a ferocious game of Frisbee without actually tossing a disc, it feels like a uniquely human satire.

	During a post-screening Q&A, director and cowriter Jesse Gouldsbury and some members of the creative team shared stories of how difficult it was to get “VelociPastor 2” made. But despite the challenges of filming a microbudget dinosaur movie, it was clear through their laughter that they wouldn’t have it any other way.

	“VelociPastor 2” is currently seeking distribution. It’s also in the middle of a series of roadshow screenings. Future dates and locations are listed on the film’s official site.

	Watch the “VelociPastor 2” trailer below.

title: Tokyo Film Festival to Reassess Its Global Standing Ahead of 40th Edition, Says Director Hisamatsu Takeo
description: The Tokyo International Film Festival will review its 39th edition once it wraps and reassess where it stands on the international circuit before i
body:
The Tokyo International Film Festival will review its 39th edition once it wraps and reassess where it stands on the international circuit before its 40th anniversary next year, festival director Hisamatsu Takeo says.

	“I believe the direction we establish through that process will also help define TIFF’s course for the next decade, leading up to its 50th edition,” Hisamatsu tells Variety.


	This year’s festival, he says, already reflects a direction the team has begun to set. The 39th edition has grown to 204 films, up from 184 last year.
	

	“We are somehow in a competitive relationship with the Busan IFF, we’re close geographically and our dates are close too. I think the time has come to re-examine where TIFF should position itself, both within Asia and within the world,” Hisamatsu says.

	The appeal of festivals such as Cannes and Venice is bound up with their host cities, he adds.

	“Tokyo has a distinctive appeal of its own: it’s a vibrant, multifaceted city where tradition and modernity coexist, and mainstream culture intersects with subculture. These are qualities we should do more to showcase to the world,” he says.

	The festival is organized by UniJapan, which also runs the TIFFCOM market and a set of international promotion and support programs. Hisamatsu, who is also UniJapan’s executive director, wants those three arms working more closely together and offering more to filmmakers and producers.

	Festivals typically don’t own the rights to the films they show, so a title’s life after Tokyo rests largely with its rights holders and distributors. Even so, Hisamatsu wants UniJapan to do more to help Japanese films that screen and win prizes at the festival take their next step.
	

	Two initiatives point in that direction. Nippon Cinema Now, the festival’s showcase for Japanese cinema, becomes a competitive section for the first time this year, with two new awards. And the new TIFF Work-in-Progress program, or TIFF-WIP, links Japanese films still in production with international festivals and industry figures, with the aim of raising their profile abroad and opening doors to overseas distribution.

	A festival, Hisamatsu says, has to balance two jobs: bringing foreign films to local audiences and taking local films overseas. Right now, he argues, the case for pushing Japanese titles abroad is strong. Japan was Country of Honor at this year’s Cannes Film Market, and more than 30 Japanese films played at the Busan International Film Festival. New talent keeps arriving, he says, and the government is backing a policy of support for the content industry as a whole, not just film.

	Even festivals billed as international, he says, are “deeply rooted in their respective countries and cultures – a purely global orientation would strip them of that character. That’s why I think the ‘glocal’ perspective will matter more and more.”

	This year’s marquee slots tilt toward mainstream entertainment, a contrast with the arthouse programming Tokyo is better known for. Zeze Takahisa’s “Sukiyaki” opens the festival, Yamazaki Takashi’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” is the centerpiece and “Train to Busan” director Yeon Sang-ho’s “Colony” closes it.

	“These films were selected on their individual merits from among the candidates we considered. It wasn’t a deliberate strategy to shift the festival’s identity in any particular direction,” Hisamatsu says.

schema.headline: Tokyo Film Festival to Reassess Its Global Standing Ahead of 40th Edition, Says Director Hisamatsu Takeo

title: Tokyo Festival’s Women’s Empowerment Lineup Follows Those Who ‘Fall Through the Cracks’
description: People pushed to move, or left without anywhere to belong, through no fault of their own form the through-line of this year’s Women’s Empowerment s
body:
People pushed to move, or left without anywhere to belong, through no fault of their own form the through-line of this year’s Women’s Empowerment section at the Tokyo International Film Festival, according to programmer Shimizu Yu, who also oversees the festival’s Youth strand.

	Now in its third year, the seven-film section includes Manuela Martelli’s “The Meltdown,” Anuparna Roy’s “Lovers in the Blue Night,” Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown” and Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming.” Also selected are Meritxell Colell Aparicio’s “Far From the Trees,” Yang Kaijing’s “Super Lucky Girl” and Muriel d’Ansembourg’s “Truly Naked.”
	

	“The films depict those who fall through the cracks of an unstable political climate or social systems – those who are struck head-on by structural contradictions, and at times exposed to crises that threaten their very dignity,” Shimizu tells Variety. “These scenes painfully strike a chord, yet I also believe there are audiences who will find their own existence affirmed through these authentic and detailed depictions of people and events as they are.”


	Shimizu is realistic about what a three-year-old program can achieve. Women’s standing has improved so little over the long sweep of human history that addressing structural problems in such a short window is extremely difficult, she says, adding that filmmaking is hard for anyone and harder still for women.

	“And yet, it is from the fact that remarkable works by women continue to be made that we draw our courage,” Shimizu says. “Precisely because this is a thematic section, I am committed to selecting films on their own merits. It is a small section, but I believe that the very scale of the challenges means there is still much we can do, and that there remains untapped potential here.”
	

	The team is putting real effort into events that run alongside the screenings, and plans to grow the section in the coming years by moving into areas TIFF has not explored before.

	“As a film festival, I believe we must more actively question our role and significance in society as an organization,” Shimizu says.

	One of those events, “Her Gaze,” this year turns to women cinematographers from Japan and Taiwan. It is overseen by Kondo Kanako, the section’s event producer, who last year spotlighted women’s film festivals in East Asia and has been looking for ways to build solidarity among women filmmakers across the region. Festivals, Kondo argues, can lift up women working in a range of positions behind the camera, and not just directors.

	“In Japan, technical roles in film have historically been dominated by men as a kind of exclusive profession, and one could argue that becoming a cinematographer is even harder than becoming a director,” Kondo says. “Now that technological advances have brought more women confidently carrying lighter cameras, I felt it was important to celebrate the pioneers of Japan and Taiwan.”

	Kondo’s background includes assistant directing, and she still works in film production staff management. Shimizu, whose own perspective comes entirely from screening practice, counts that hands-on knowledge of filmmaking as one of the section’s strengths.

	Shimizu has also programmed experimental cinema at the International Film Festival Rotterdam, where the work included collaborating with DINAMO, an international network of experimental film distributors and archives. That experience continues to shape her approach to archival material.

	“Women have long been treated as objects of the gaze within cinema, and I believe experimental film carries within it a resistance to being consumed simply through being watched,” Shimizu says. “Many women filmmakers are highly conscious of this, and work that rises to the challenge with an awareness of the great history of film is always one of the key criteria I prioritize in selecting films.”

	On the youth side, the TIFF Teens filmmaking workshop marks its 10th anniversary this year. Shimizu notes that everyone carries a different idea of what cinema is, and that films made with a theater in mind are becoming unfamiliar to many. The three titles in this year’s Youth section – Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” María Aparicio’s “Sometimes Sadness, Sometimes Rebellion” and Lorenzo Ferro and Lucas A. Vignale’s “The River Train” – were picked to make audiences rethink the medium.
	

	“Moving images have become more familiar and abundant than ever, but I believe these three are works that can only truly be received in cinemas,” Shimizu says.

	She sees possibility in something a regular theatrical release cannot offer: the chance at a festival to encounter “not only what you set out to see, but also the surprising, and at times the irregular.” Like Women’s Empowerment, the Youth section runs its own slate of events designed to give the films context.

	“Our goal is for each individual audience member to experience a richer moment through cinema,” Shimizu says. “And perhaps, as a result, some of them may go on to work in the world of film.”

schema.headline: Tokyo Festival’s Women’s Empowerment Lineup Follows Those Who ‘Fall Through the Cracks’

title: Korea Box Office: Anime Phenomenon ‘Chiikawa’ Remains Unstoppable as Yeon Sang-ho Thriller ‘Paradise Lost’ Debuts
description: Japanese animated sensation “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” maintained a commanding grip on the South Korean box office over
body:
Japanese animated sensation “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” maintained a commanding grip on the South Korean box office over the weekend of Oct. 23–25, capturing nearly 45% of nationwide ticket revenue in its fourth frame. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, the Toho-distributed fantasy release took in $2.5 million from 320,293 admissions across 1,115 screens, accounting for 44.7% of the weekend market.
	

	Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the popular manga by Nagano, the fantasy feature tracks the small protagonist and companions journeying to a scenic coastal island before uncovering a sinister local mystery. Driven by enduring youth and family turnout, the animated blockbuster pushed its cumulative South Korean haul to $17.5 million from 2,248,137 total admissions since launching on Sep. 30.


	Director Hur Jin-ho’s political thriller “The Assassin(s)” held second place, earning $520,822 from 68,241 admissions across 730 screens to capture 9.2% of the frame. Distributed by Hive Media Corp, the period drama reconstructs the August 15, 1974 assassination attempt on President Park Chung-hee and stars Yu Hae-jin, Park Hae-il, and Lee Min-ho investigating irregularities surrounding the inquiry into the death of First Lady Yuk Young-soo.

	The production’s theatrical run continues against persistent political blowback and legal challenges, with conservative civic groups and bereaved family members lodging defamation complaints alleging historical distortion over its depiction of state involvement. Despite protests that previously prompted 19 film guilds to issue a joint statement defending cinematic freedom, the release lifted its cume to $25 million from 3,374,517 admissions since its Sep. 23 rollout.
	

	CJ Entertainment’s psychological thriller “Paradise Lost” opened in third place, generating $502,962 from 66,699 admissions across 803 screens for an 8.9% market share. Directed and co-written by Yeon Sang-ho and starring Kim Hyun-joo and Bae Hyun-sung, the mystery follows a desperate mother navigating a closed religious community while searching for her missing son. Following its world premiere at Toronto and an Oct. 21 mid-week rollout, the title has accumulated $769,865 from 104,877 total admissions.

	Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” debuted in fourth place, collecting $388,947 from 48,245 admissions across 655 screens for 6.9% of the market. Since opening on Oct. 21, the film has grossed $595,460 from 77,153 viewers.

	CJ ENM’s gambling drama “Tazza: The Song of Beelzebub” took fifth place in its fifth weekend, taking in $371,743 from 46,919 admissions across 618 screens to claim 6.6% of receipts. Directed by Choi Kook-hee and starring Byun Yo-han, Noh Jae-won, and Ayaka Miyoshi, the fourth installment in the franchise pushed its gross to $15.3 million and stands on the brink of two million tickets at 1,999,477 admissions.

	Plus M Entertainment’s period drama “Still Shining” opened in sixth place, earning $148,298 from 21,564 admissions across 562 screens. Directed by Song Il-gon and starring veteran actor Kim Hye-ja alongside Cha Mi-kyung, the drama traces the lifelong bond between two women who promised to sing together in Seoul during the Japanese colonial era. Counting mid-week business since its Oct. 21 debut, the release has taken $278,527 from 41,037 viewers.

	Universal’s tentpole “The Odyssey” placed seventh in its twelfth weekend, drawing $164,558 from 20,189 admissions across 341 screens. Its cumulative haul reached $106.2 million from 12,311,245 admissions since opening on Aug. 5.

	Amazon MGM Studios and Warner Bros.’ psychological thriller “Verity” opened in eighth place, pulling in $120,876 from 16,416 admissions across 458 screens and has grossed $178,096 from 25,190 admissions since its Oct. 22 bow.

	Director Kore-eda Hirokazu’s live-action manga drama “Look Back” took ninth place in its third weekend, earning $126,854 from 15,624 admissions across 190 screens, lifting its cumulative total to $1 million from 131,051 admissions.
	

	Rounding out the top 10 was domestic action thriller “Killing Time” with $82,439 from 11,244 admissions across 274 screens. Directed by Jang Jun-yeob and starring Ryu Hye-young and Nam Yoon-su, the film centers on a popular YouTube crew that collapses overnight after an accident claims a member’s life during a live broadcast; when they stage an extreme comeback stunt to regain fame, mysterious figures force them into a real, deadly survival game. Since its Oct. 21 release, the thriller has grossed $135,388 from 19,121 viewers.

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $5.6 million, down from last week’s $6.7 million.

title: Anime’s Pay Divide Runs Between Studios That Take Risks and Those That Don’t, Says Tokyo Festival Advisor
description: Japan’s anime industry is in better shape overall, but gaps in pay and conditions are opening up largely between studios prepared to put their own
body:
Japan’s anime industry is in better shape overall, but gaps in pay and conditions are opening up largely between studios prepared to put their own capital on the line and those that are not, according to Fujitsu Ryota, programming advisor for the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Animation section.

	“Given the high level of creativity demonstrated by animation professionals, their compensation is still not where it should be,” Fujitsu tells Variety.
	

	He describes the link between hits and pay as a chicken-and-egg problem. As overseas demand for anime grows, the companies that can pay production staff properly, and so draw the talent they need, look best placed to make strong work and build a global presence.


	“In other words, it’s not necessarily that a hit film generates profits that are then passed on to the people who made it. Rather, companies that can attract the right people in the first place are better positioned to produce a hit,” Fujitsu says.

	That requires studios to commit more of their own money and shoulder bigger business risks, he adds. Some can. Others can’t.

	“How to bridge that gap depends on how individual companies choose to run their businesses,” he says. “If we simply lump everything together as an ‘industry-wide problem,’ we risk obscuring the specific factors at play.”

	The Animation section this year features nine new Japanese and international works. On the Japanese side, auteur projects from major studios with commercial track records, Nishigori Atsushi’s “Grotesqqque” and Natsume Shingo’s “Ghost – End of Night,” sit alongside independent productions, Kadowaki Kohei’s “We Are Aliens” and Kawajiri Masanao’s “Cherry and Virgin.” The international slate includes Louis Clichy’s “Iron Boy,” Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado’s “Forgotten Island” and “Walking with Animators,” a documentary by Alexandre Poncet and Gilles Penso about the making of animated films.
	

	“I don’t see commercial and experimental works as opposing forces. There is a broad spectrum between the two, and many films fall somewhere along it,” Fujitsu says.

	The four Japanese titles, he argues, may be closer in genre than their production setups would suggest. Placing them side by side is meant to make audiences ask whether a line between commercial and experimental animation exists at all, and the same goes for the international picks.

	“Ultimately, what we’re looking for in TIFF’s Animation section are films with a distinct creative signature – works that make the creators’ voices visible and offer audiences something stimulating in a variety of ways,” he says.

	The section also runs a focus on women animation directors, with Nagaoka Chika’s “Detective Conan: The Fist of Blue Sapphire,” Watanabe Kotono’s “Gold Kingdom and Water Kingdom” and Yoshimura Ai’s “The Rose of Versailles.” The program has been under consideration for some time, Fujitsu says, and its aim is not to pin down what women bring to animation that was previously absent. Rather, it reflects an industry in which the number of women directors is clearly set to grow.

	“There might be a slight paradox here, but we’re focusing on women directors precisely because we’re in a transitional period, moving toward a point where there will no longer be a need to single them out as women directors,” he says.

	Women have directed animation in Japan since the 1980s, Fujitsu notes, but their ranks began to swell in the 2000s, partly because more women joined production teams throughout the business.

	With streamers pouring money into anime and theatrical franchises drawing huge crowds, Fujitsu says the risk that original features without established IP will find it harder to get financed and distributed is definitely there.

	“In a way, the efforts we’re seeing to develop original animated films are also attempts to prevent that future from becoming a reality,” he says.

	Public money for animated features in Japan is scarce, which makes originals hard to finance. More Japanese animated films have reached international festivals in recent years, he says, and while that partly reflects festivals’ own tastes, Japanese professionals’ growing interest in festivals, overseas markets and co-productions is opening routes around the funding problem.
	

	Fujitsu is also moderating a discussion at TIFFCOM, the festival’s content market, on launching a new international anime award in 2027. In conversations with the team behind Tokyo Anime Next, he says, they agreed that an award should be “an inspiring message for creators – something that makes them go, ‘Ah, that makes sense!’ – as well as a breath of fresh air for the festival, the kind that makes people say, ‘Oh, such a film exists!’”

	He hopes the Tokyo Anime Next award becomes an occasion for people across the animation business to come together and celebrate the year’s work, giving both professionals and fans a sense of recognition.

	“Given that an award of this kind has not existed before, I think it could play a significant role, not only by recognizing outstanding works, but also by bringing individual members of the production teams into the spotlight,” Fujitsu says.

title: John Oliver Issues Urgent Warning Ahead of Midterms About the Republican Party’s Nazi Ties
description: John Oliver returned to the “Last Week Tonight” desk after a two-week absence and focused the entirety of Sunday night’s episode on a “worrying tre
body:
John Oliver returned to the “Last Week Tonight” desk after a two-week absence and focused the entirety of Sunday night’s episode on a “worrying trend that’s been on the rise” amongst the Republican Party ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections — their apparent affinity for Nazis.

	There is Peter Oberacker, a Republican candidate for New York’s 19th congressional district. Back in 2015, Oberacker posted a photo to Facebook on Veterans Day memorializing his late grandfather — in full Wehrmacht uniform — who’d died fighting for Nazi Germany. Oberacker later claimed it was the only photo of his grandfather that he had.
	

	“Yeah, not great!” exclaimed Oliver. “If that is the only picture that you have, maybe consider having no pictures of him! You can sit Veterans Day out. No one will think that’s weird.”


	The HBO host then brought up how Elon Musk delivered what very much appeared to be a Nazi salute to Trump supporters at a rally following his election in 2025.

	“Everything about that screams, ‘Nazi!’” said Oliver, adding, “Well, almost everything. To be fair to the Nazis, unlike Elon, they at least looked sharp in their suits.”

	He continued, claiming, “It does feel that the Republican Party has been getting way too comfortable with some, at best, Nazi-adjacent shit,” including Paul Ingrassia, Trump’s nominee to the Office of Special Counsel, who withdrew his nomination after leaked group chat messages revealed him saying, “I do have a Nazi streak in me from time to time, I will admit it.” And Brandon Herrera, a Republican nominee for Texas’s 23rd congressional district, who posted a YouTube video in 2022 where he referred to the MP-40 as “Hitler’s street sweeper” followed by footage of him and a friend goose-stepping to a Nazi marching song.
	

	Even Karl Rove, the architect of George W. Bush’s presidency, issued a warning last month at the Texas Tribune Festival that his party was being taken over by “bigots” like Bo French, a candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner known for racist social media posts, adding, “Nick Fuentes goes to Dallas and meets with a bunch of Republican leaders. This guy is a Nazi.”

	Oliver argued that Israel’s war in Gaza has led “some on the far-right to seize on this moment and elevate antisemitic conspiracy theories,” including Tucker Carlson’s warm podcast interview with the Hitler-worshipping neo-Nazi Fuentes. The Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts defended Carlson’s chummy interview with Fuentes and said the podcaster was under attack from “globalist forces,” later walking back the defense by claiming that he, the leader of the top conservative think tank, doesn’t pay attention to the news.

	Fuentes claimed on his podcast that “whites built everything” and “Jews are money-changers, bullshit artists, psychopaths, charlatans, grifters, manipulators… why do you think they’re so obnoxious? Why do you think they’re so fucking obnoxious? They have no manners because they’re from the third world. They come from the literal ghetto.”

	Cue Oliver: “It makes it all the more laughable that Tucker made such a show of offering Fuentes, a man who’s literally spent thousands of hours on the internet saying whatever he wants, the chance to finally say what he thinks… And the worrying thing is, it’s not just Tucker. Fuentes has been inching closer and closer to mainstream Republicans over the years,” such as GOP Congressman Paul Gosar, who gave the keynote speech at Fuentes’s America First Political Action Conference in 2021 and Marjorie Taylor Greene, who did the same in 2022. Trump also infamously dined with Fuentes at Mar-a-Lago in November 2022, and none other than Kanye West brought him there — one month after West tweeted, “I’m going death con 3 On JEWISH PEOPLE.”

	“Nazis getting power doesn’t historically bode well for anyone, including, for what it’s worth, Nazis, who didn’t exactly have the best 1945,” reasoned Oliver, who further highlighted the Republican Party’s “groyper problem” by pointing to a Manhattan Institute analysis of the GOP that determined, “Nearly four in ten in the current GOP (37%) believe the Holocaust was greatly exaggerated or did not happen as historians described,” including “54% of men under 50.” The comedian then pointed to the leaked group chats from leaders of Young Republican groups around the country praising Hitler and spouting racial epithets left and right.
	

	“There are some who will say, ‘Calm down. This seems to be just a bunch of kids and shitty streamers. You can just ignore it,’” said Oliver, which is something JD Vance argued when he was asked about the group chat, saying, “Kids do stupid things.” They weren’t kids, though, but rather full-grown adults in their 20s and 30s.

	“The far-right fringe currently rising up in this party is not remotely new, from the John Birch Society through Barry Goldwater and Pat Buchanan, the Republican Party has always left its door ajar for bigots, cranks and conspiracy theorists,” asserted Oliver. “Have you ever listened to the Nixon Tapes? They would do numbers on Rumble today.”

	Other sketchy GOP candidates include Marshall Rawson, running for Florida House District 10, who marched with neo-Nazis in Charlottesville. Oliver brought up how, when 28 GOP officials were asked if they’d denounced Rawson given his neo-Nazi ties, only three responded, and two of them stood by Rawson.

	“The point here is: Far-right views in the Republican Party are by no means irrelevant and they are way past the point of being ignorable —some of them are literally on the ballot in nine days, in an election, by the way, where the single biggest campaign spender is [Elon Musk], you know, of the Adolf-aloha wave.”

schema.headline: John Oliver Issues Urgent Warning Ahead of Midterms About the Republican Party’s Nazi Ties

title: ‘Saiyaara’ Star Ahaan Panday and Sharvari’s Ali Abbas Zafar Romantic Action-Drama for Yash Raj Films Unveils Title (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Ali Abbas Zafar’s romantic action-drama pairing “Saiyaara” breakout Ahaan Panday with Sharvari will be called “Beparwah,” Yash Raj Films revealed M
body:
Ali Abbas Zafar’s romantic action-drama pairing “Saiyaara” breakout Ahaan Panday with Sharvari will be called “Beparwah,” Yash Raj Films revealed Monday.

	The title reveal came exactly five months before the film opens worldwide in theaters on March 26, 2027, the Good Friday holiday. Aditya Chopra produces. “Beparwah” is the first time Panday and Sharvari have shared the screen.


	Until Monday, the film had been known only as Zafar’s untitled next. Yash Raj Films first set the March 2027 date in July, while the production was shooting in the U.K., where much of the film was made.
	

	“Beparwah” reunites Zafar with Chopra for a fifth time. Their earlier collaborations were romantic comedy “Mere Brother Ki Dulhan” (2011), crime drama “Gunday” (2014), wrestling drama “Sultan” (2016) and spy thriller “Tiger Zinda Hai” (2017). The last two, both toplined by Salman Khan, were blockbusters for the banner. Zafar co-wrote the script with Chopra.


	Since “Tiger Zinda Hai,” Zafar has directed Khan again in “Bharat” (2019), created the Prime Video political series “Tandav” (2021) and helmed “Bade Miyan Chote Miyan” (2024), an Akshay Kumar and Tiger Shroff action vehicle.

	Panday made his screen debut in Mohit Suri’s “Saiyaara,” a YRF musical romance opposite fellow newcomer Aneet Padda that became one of the biggest Bollywood hits of 2025. It grossed more than $65 million worldwide and became the highest-grossing Indian love story on record. Panday is the nephew of actor Chunky Panday and a cousin of actor Ananya Panday.
	

	Sharvari launched her career in YRF’s “Bunty Aur Babli 2” (2021) and broke through with the 2024 horror-comedy “Munjya,” which crossed $14 million at the box office. This July, she starred opposite Alia Bhatt in “Alpha,” the first female-led entry in YRF’s spy universe franchise.

	The “Beparwah” cast also includes Bobby Deol, Sharvari’s “Alpha” co-star, and Aaishvary Thackeray, grandson of Shiv Sena party founder Bal Thackeray, who plays the antagonist.

	Founded in 1970 by the late Yash Chopra and now run by his son Aditya, YRF is one of India’s leading studios. Its spy universe, which includes Zafar’s “Tiger Zinda Hai,” also spans the “War” and “Pathaan” films.

title: Family Dramas Dominate Tokyo Festival’s Asian Lineup Amid ‘Geopolitical Volatility’
description: Family relationships run through the Asian films that Tokyo International Film Festival programmer Ishizaka Kenji has picked for this year’s editio
body:
Family relationships run through the Asian films that Tokyo International Film Festival programmer Ishizaka Kenji has picked for this year’s edition.

	“While it is hard to pinpoint an exact catalyst for this surge in family-driven drama, what is undeniable is that amidst today’s geopolitical volatility, these filmmakers share an instinctive urge to reexamine the smallest foundational unit around them: the family and sibling bonds,” Ishizaka tells Variety.
	

	Ishizaka has programmed Asian cinema at the festival since 2007, when most submissions were still shot on film. Digital took over within a few years. His selection process moved from 35mm prints and VHS tapes to DVDs, and later to streaming links and downloadable screeners.


	‘The physical medium gave way to data; cinema lost its tangible ‘weight,” he says.

	The shift also changed what films looked like. Freed from the need to reload film, Asian directors leaned into long running times built on unbroken takes, and so-called slow cinema spread across the region. Two of its leading auteurs took top prizes at major European festivals in the 2010s: Thailand’s Apichatpong Weerasethakul won the Palme d’Or at Cannes for “Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives,” and the Philippines’ Lav Diaz won Venice’s Golden Lion for “The Woman Who Left.”

	Ishizaka also oversees Asian Future, the festival’s competition for young Asian filmmakers. Its 10 titles this year include Katski Flores’ “Edjop” from the Philippines, Kim Hyun-min’s “On the Heights” from South Korea and Chezhiyan’s “The Paper Flower” from India. Azamat Shargyn’s “Shyrmauyq” from Kazakhstan, Ariani Darmawan’s “Jani Be Good” from Indonesia and Kujiraoka Hironori’s “Saravah” from Japan are also in the running.
	

	The line between studio fare and independent film has blurred considerably, he says.

	“In the Philippines, for instance – a national cinema often described as enjoying its ‘Third Golden Age’ since 2005 – we are seeing mainstream stars actively board indie projects after falling in love with bold, original scripts,” Ishizaka says. “This has even spawned the portmanteau ‘maindie’ cinema.”

	He points to directors Brillante Mendoza and Jun Robles Lana, who switch easily between commercial and small-scale indie work, as key links between the two worlds. Other industries in the region are seeing similar crossover.

	If the 2010s belonged to Southeast Asian cinema, the story of the 2020s is still being written. For now, Ishizaka singles out Taiwan and South Korea for the strength of their public funding and institutional backing.

	“Thematically, an exciting wave of emerging filmmakers from China’s autonomous regions – Tibet, Inner Mongolia, and Xinjiang – is stepping into the spotlight,” he says. “Mentored and inspired by trailblazing predecessors like the late Pema Tseden, these directors bring distinct regional perspectives and aesthetic sensibilities that set them apart from mainstream Chinese cinema.”

	For emerging directors in Asian Future, Ishizaka says, the reactions of Tokyo audiences feed straight into their next projects, while meetings with visiting international programmers regularly lead to invitations from other festivals and co-production opportunities. Japan’s network of independent arthouse venues, known locally as mini-theaters, is supported by experienced distributors of international cinema.

	“It is not uncommon for a festival premiere here to translate directly into a domestic theatrical distribution deal,” Ishizaka says. “Ultimately, our mission is to serve as an active springboard that fosters these industry connections.”

	Ishizaka has spent much of his career studying documentary film and cultural exchange between Asia and the Middle East. Although Asian Future has no nonfiction titles this year, he sees a dramatic change in war documentaries from across Asia in the last five years.

	“Miniature digital cameras mounted on helmets capture the harrowing frontline experience with visceral immediacy, yielding footage so intense it transcends realism into what can only be called the ‘hyper-real,’” he says. “It is the visual language of an era marked by conflict.”
	

	Fiction features tackling the same subjects, by contrast, appear to be moving toward metaphor and allegory, he says.

schema.headline: Family Dramas Dominate Tokyo Festival’s Asian Lineup Amid ‘Geopolitical Volatility’

Philippine Official

            A Philippine official says the investigation into Thomas Markle Sr.'s alleged possession of child abuse material points to a sex offender of the "grossest kind" -- confirming authorities uncovered illicit images during their search.
      
    
            Philippine interior minister Jonvic Remulla told The Guardian that authorities found a "trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop" at Thomas Sr.'s home.
      
    
            Remulla added ... "In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles. Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After Thomas Sr.'s son, Thomas Markle Jr., came forward to report his father to authorities ... Thomas Sr. denied the claims against him, calling them "bulls***."
      
    
            Thomas Jr. had told The Sun that he discovered "hundreds, if not thousands" of alleged child sex abuse images before reporting his father to authorities.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Meghan Markle said that she previously received a letter containing similar claims ... and since her statement, London's Met Police confirmed forwarding a letter with "several claims" about her father to Meghan in 2019.

            Following receipt of the note ...             In an explosive interview with The Mail on Sunday ... Thomas Sr. acknowledged Meghan and her family had cut contact with him ... but claimed he didn't have a chance to refute the claims.
      
    
            Thomas Sr. has also denied ever sleeping with anyone underage.
